America's Iran War: A Six-Month Startup Burning Cash With No Product

The pitch deck promised a quick knockout. Six months in, Washington's Iran venture is running out of runway, the founder's still promising "very hard" hits, and the board — that is, America's allies — is quietly shopping for a new CEO to hedge against.

Trump's version of the roadmap hasn't changed: "We'll be hitting them. We'll be hitting them very hard," followed by the classic founder optimism that Iran will eventually crack — "At some point, they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore'". 

Six months of "they'll get weaker, then they peter out," and the Strait of Hormuz is, per the analysts actually paying attention, effectively under Iranian control.

Robin Niblett, former Chatham House director, delivers the investor memo nobody wanted: "For U.S. allies and those who rely on the U.S. for security, this is confirmation that you can't trust the United States... 

Now America has confirmed itself as a force of disorder and everyone is drawing lessons from it, and trying to be less dependent." Translation: the shareholders are pulling out before the next funding round.

Meanwhile the Patriots — the missile kind, not the patriotism kind — are running dry, a shortage already starving Ukraine and broadcasting to Moscow and Beijing that America's global-reach subscription has lapsed.

 Aaron David Miller sums up the balance sheet: the war "has undermined U.S. deterrence and credibility, antagonized America's allies and delighted its adversaries," adding that if the strait ends up under Iranian veto, "it will constitute nothing less than a strategic defeat."

Israel isn't spared the audit either — American officials, including Vice President JD Vance, are quietly briefing that Netanyahu oversold the "quick and decisive" pitch that got Trump into this in the first place. Two allies, one failing venture, and a very familiar blame-the-cofounder routine.

Iran, for its part, isn't interested in a handshake deal with a partner who tore up the last two contracts. It wants the Hormuz terms locked before it even discusses a new memorandum — because as one Iran analyst put it, Tehran's calculus is "simple": leverage now, or get burned again later.

So: is this a war Washington doesn't know how to win, or one it never actually knew how to end — and does anyone in the building still remember which?
